working: A sum of 6 with n dice needs compositions of 6 into n parts each between 1 and 6 (the upper bound never binds here). 4 dice: C(5,3) = 10 of 6^4 = 1296. 3 dice: C(5,2) = 10 of 216. 2 dice: 5 of 36. So the probabilities are 10/1296, 10/216, 5/36; multiplying all three by 1296 gives 10 : 60 : 180 = 1 : 6 : 18, in the stated order 4, 3, 2 dice. Counts verified by exhaustive enumeration.

working: The product ends in 1, 3, 7 or 9 exactly when it is odd and not divisible by 5, which forces every factor's last digit into {1,3,7,9} (any factor ending in an even digit makes the product even; any ending in 5 makes it end in 5 or 0). Each factor's last digit is one of 10 equally likely digits, so the probability is (4/10)^4 = (2/5)^4 = 16/625. Verified by enumerating all 10^4 last-digit combinations: 256/10000 = 16/625.

notes: The stem prints the denominator's z carrying a DOT accent (pandoc 'overset dot over z'), which is not standard notation in a complex-locus problem -- a dot over z is a time derivative, meaningless here. I read it as plain z, the standard anthologised form of this problem, which yields the straight line x + 2y - 2 = 0. If instead the dot is a mangled CONJUGATE bar, i.e. Im((2z+1)/(i*conj(z)+1)) = -2, the same rationalisation gives -x + 4y^2 + 6y + 2 = 0, i.e. x = 4y^2 + 6y + 2, a PARABOLA -- option C. working: A determinant equals that of its transpose, so A = |a b c; d e f; l m n|. B = |l m n; a b c; d e f| is that same matrix with its rows cyclically shifted (third row brought to the top), a 3-cycle and therefore an even permutation, so the determinant is unchanged: B = A and A - B = 0. Verified symbolically (A - B expands to 0, while A + B is twice a non-zero general expression, so option A fails).
